narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 51% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. At 23, it sits well below the average of 37 among students who were admitted, signaling weaker preparation in the eyes of the model.

Your family income bracket came next. Being in the lower-middle income group actually worked in your favor and pulled the prediction slightly toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the other factors.

Your first-year law school grades ranked third. Placing in the fourth decile (compared to an average of sixth decile among accepted students) also nudged the outcome toward failure, though less forcefully than your LSAT.

Taken together, the model saw your lower LSAT and weaker early grades as the dominant signals that you were more likely than not to struggle with the bar exam. 

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model flagged. Retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score, while also improving your academic performance in the coming year. These improvements would directly address the biggest reasons for the rejection and could change the outcome if you reapply. (218 words)
